cues.text: A Young Friar Already Renowned
By 1227, St. Anthony of Padua was still only in his early thirties.
Yet he had already become one of Italy’s most sought-after preachers, renowned for such thorough knowledge of Scripture that he would later be named a Doctor of the Church.

His preaching that year had drawn him to Rimini, a city where, tradition holds, an Albigensian heretic known as Bonovillo openly denied the Church's teaching on the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist.
A Public Challenge
According to the earliest surviving biography of the saint, known as L'Assidua , Bonovillo confronted Anthony directly.

He declared that he would renounce his heresy only if a mule he had deliberately starved for three days, when set before both fodder and a consecrated host, would choose to adore the host rather than eat.
Anthony accepted the public challenge without hesitation.
The Mule Kneels
On the appointed day, before a crowd gathered in the public square, tradition holds that Anthony emerged with the Blessed Sacrament.
He addressed the starving animal directly: "In the name of your Creator, whom I, unworthy as I am, hold in my hands, I command you to come forward and pay reverence."
Bonovillo then set fodder before the mule.
Despite its hunger, the account says, the animal ignored the food entirely and instead approached the saint, bending its front legs in reverence before the host.
A Heretic's Conversion, and a Lasting Shrine
Bonovillo, true to his public word, is said to have abandoned his heresy on the spot and become one of Anthony's most devoted supporters from that day forward.
A shrine was later built on the site of the miracle, and the church that stands there today, in the heart of Rimini, still draws visitors who come to venerate the memory of the event.
The episode is recorded not only in L'Assidua but in the Benignitas , another of the earliest surviving lives of the saint.
By medieval hagiographic standards, this places it among the better-attested Eucharistic traditions associated with a named and thoroughly documented saint.
Legacy
We find in the Miracle of Rimini a distinctive shape among Eucharistic accounts: not a private doubt resolved quietly, nor a desecration exposed.
Instead, it was a very public contest willingly accepted by a saint confident enough in the Real Presence to stake a heretic's conversion on its outcome.
Anthony’s willingness to be tested so openly, and his challenger’s swiftness in honoring his own word once the sign was given, together offer a model of debate.
It was settled not by argument alone, but by a shared willingness to let the truth show itself.
